claims.text: NbTaTiV is a refractory, single-solid-solution BCC high-entropy alloy.
Toughness retention in NbTaTiV is governed by the dominant dislocation mechanism.
Promoting edge-dislocation activity over screw-dislocation activity improves toughness.
The as-processed alloy has a mixed dislocation population at room temperature.
At room temperature, the dislocation population in NbTaTiV is biased toward screw dislocations.
The room-temperature screw-dislocation bias correlates with lower toughness.
Raising the deformation temperature to around 600 °C promotes edge-dominated plasticity in NbTaTiV.
Edge dislocations in BCC high-entropy alloys are less rate-sensitive than screw dislocations.
Edge-dislocation activity promotes more uniform plastic deformation.
Edge-dislocation-dominated plasticity causes NbTaTiV to retain higher toughness.
Screw-dislocation dominance can cause core pinning and brittleness.
At around 600 °C, the proportion or mobility of edge dislocations will increase relative to room temperature.
The elevated-temperature increase in edge-dislocation activity will correlate with increased tensile ductility and favorable work-hardening behavior.
Tensile ductility and work-hardening behavior are suitable indicators of toughness retention.
The proposed behavior applies to refractory BCC high-entropy alloys, specifically NbTaTiV, at moderate strain rates.
The mechanism should remain governing up to approximately 600 °C, above which diffusion-driven phase changes may become significant.
Elevated-temperature phase instabilities or diffusion effects could confound the relationship between dislocation character and toughness.
Room-temperature and 600 °C tensile tests at fixed strain rate, with dislocation and phase characterization, constitute the proposed controlled intervention.
A joint absence of increased edge-dislocation activity and improved toughness indicators at 600 °C is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
